arXiv:1501.05168v1 [math.AG] 21 Jan 2015

Quasi-translations and singular Hessians

Michiel de Bondt
Abstract

In 1876 in [8], the authors Paul Gordan and Max Nöther classify all homogeneous polynomials hh in at most five variables for which the Hessian determinant vanishes. For that purpose, they study quasi-translations which are associated with singular Hessians.

We will explain what quasi-translations are and formulate some elementary properties of them. Additionally, we classify all quasi-translations with Jacobian rank one and all so-called irreducible homogeneous quasi-translations with Jacobian rank two. The latter is an important result of [8]. Using these results, we classify all quasi-translations in dimension at most three and all homogeneous quasi-translations in dimension at most four.

Furthermore, we describe the connection of quasi-translation with singular Hessians, and as an application, we will classify all polynomials in dimension two and all homogeneous polynomials in dimensions three and four whose Hessian determinant vanishes. More precisely, we will show that up to linear terms, these polynomials can be expressed in n−1n-1 linear forms, where nn is the dimension, according to an invalid theorem of Hesse.

In the last section, we formulate some known results and conjectures in connection with quasi-translations and singular Hessians.

Key words:

Quasi-translation, Hessian, determinant zero, homogeneous, locally nilpotent derivation, algebraic dependence, linear dependence.

MSC 2010:

14R05, 14R10, 14R20, 13N15.

1 Quasi-translations

Let AA be a commutative ring with ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} and nn be a positive natural number. Write

x=(x1x2⋮xn)=(x1,x2,…,xn)x=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x_{1}\\ x_{2}\\ \vdots\\ x_{n}\end{array}\right)=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})

for the identity map from AnA^{n} to AnA^{n}, thus x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} are variables that correspond to the coordinates of AnA^{n}. A translation of AnA^{n} is a map

x+c=(x1+c1x2+c2⋮xn+cn)x+c=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x_{1}+c_{1}\\ x_{2}+c_{2}\\ \vdots\\ x_{n}+c_{n}\end{array}\right)

where c∈Anc\in A^{n} is a fixed vector. For a translation x+cx+c, we have that x−cx-c is the inverse polynomial map, because

(x−c)∘(x+c)=((x1+c1)−c1(x2+c2)−c2⋮(xn+cn)−cn)=(x1x2⋮xn)=x(x-c)\circ(x+c)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}(x_{1}+c_{1})-c_{1}\\ (x_{2}+c_{2})-c_{2}\\ \vdots\\ (x_{n}+c_{n})-c_{n}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x_{1}\\ x_{2}\\ \vdots\\ x_{n}\end{array}\right)=x

is the identity map.

Inspired by this property, we define a quasi-translation as a polynomial map

x+H=(x1+H1x2+H2⋮xn+Hn)=(x1+H1​(x)x2+H2​(x)⋮xn+Hn​(x))x+H=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x_{1}+H_{1}\\ x_{2}+H_{2}\\ \vdots\\ x_{n}+H_{n}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x_{1}+H_{1}(x)\\ x_{2}+H_{2}(x)\\ \vdots\\ x_{n}+H_{n}(x)\end{array}\right)

such that x−Hx-H is the inverse polynomial map of x+Hx+H, i.e.

(x−H)∘(x+H)=((x1+H1​(x))−H1​(x+H)(x2+H2​(x))−H2​(x+H)⋮(xn+Hn​(x))−Hn​(x+H))=x(x-H)\circ(x+H)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\big(x_{1}+H_{1}(x)\big)-H_{1}(x+H)\\ \big(x_{2}+H_{2}(x)\big)-H_{2}(x+H)\\ \vdots\\ \big(x_{n}+H_{n}(x)\big)-H_{n}(x+H)\\ \end{array}\right)=x

The difference between a translation x+cx+c and a quasi-translation x+Hx+H is that ci∈Ac_{i}\in A for all ii, while Hi∈A⁡[x]=A⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]H_{i}\in A[x]=A[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}] for all ii.

For a regular translation x+cx+c, we have that applying it mm times comes down to the translation x+m​cx+mc. If f∈ℂ⁡[x]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] is an invariant of a regular translation x+cx+c, i.e. f⁡(x+c)=f⁡(x)f(x+c)=f(x), then f⁡(x+(m+1)​c)=f⁡(x+m​c)f(x+(m+1)c)=f(x+mc) follows by substituting x=x+m​cx=x+mc, whence by induction on mm, f⁡(x+m​c)=f⁡(x)f(x+mc)=f(x) for all m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}. Below, we show similar results for quasi-translations.

Since (x−H)∘(x+H)=x(x-H)\circ(x+H)=x, we see that

(x+m​H)∘(x+H)\displaystyle(x+mH)\circ(x+H) =((m+1)​x−m⁡(x−H))∘(x+H)\displaystyle=\big((m+1)x-m(x-H)\big)\circ(x+H)
=(m+1)​(x+H)−m​x=x+(m+1)​H\displaystyle=(m+1)(x+H)-mx=x+(m+1)H

Hence it follows by induction on mm that applying x+Hx+H mm times comes down to the map x+m​Hx+mH indeed. Consequently, if f∈A⁡[x]f\in A[x] is an invariant of a x+Hx+H, i.e. f⁡(x+H)=f⁡(x)f(x+H)=f(x), then

f(x+mH)=f((x+H)∘⋯∘(x+H))=f(x)f(x+mH)=f((x+H)\circ\cdots\circ(x+H))=f(x)

follows for each m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}} by applying f⁡(x+H)=f⁡(x)f(x+H)=f(x) mm times. Thus

f⁡(x+H)=f⁡(x)⟹f⁡(x+m​H)=f⁡(x)​ for all m∈Nf(x+H)=f(x)\Longrightarrow f(x+mH)=f(x)\mbox{ for all $m\in N$} (1.1)

With some techniques ‘on the shelf’, we can improve (1.1) to the following.

Lemma 1.1.

Assume that x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation over AA. Then

f⁡(x+H)=f⁡(x)⟹f⁡(x+t​H)=f⁡(x)f(x+H)=f(x)\Longrightarrow f(x+tH)=f(x) (1.2)

where tt is a new indeterminate.

Proof.

Let d:=deg⁡fd:=\deg f and write f⁡(x+t​H)−f=cd​td+cd−1​td−1+⋯+c1​t+c0f(x+tH)-f=c_{d}t^{d}+c_{d-1}t^{d-1}+\cdots+c_{1}t+c_{0}. Since f⁡(x+m​H)−f=0f(x+mH)-f=0 for all m∈{0,1,2,…,d}m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,d\} on account of (1.1),

(1002⋯0d1112⋯1d1222⋯2d⋮⋮⋮⋱⋮1dd2⋯dd)⋅(c0c1c2⋮cd)=(000⋮0)\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}1&0&0^{2}&\cdots&0^{d}\\ 1&1&1^{2}&\cdots&1^{d}\\ 1&2&2^{2}&\cdots&2^{d}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ 1&d&d^{2}&\cdots&d^{d}\end{array}\right)\cdot\left(\begin{array}[]{c}c_{0}\\ c_{1}\\ c_{2}\\ \vdots\\ c_{d}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ 0\\ 0\\ \vdots\\ 0\end{array}\right)

The matrix on the left hand side is of Hadamard type and hence invertible, because A⊇ℚA\supseteq{\mathbb{Q}}. Consequently, c0=c1=c2=⋯=cd=0c_{0}=c_{1}=c_{2}=\cdots=c_{d}=0. Hence f⁡(x+t​H)=ff(x+tH)=f, as desired. ∎

But Gordan and Nöther did not use the term quasi-translation, and characterized quasi-translations in another way. To describe it, we define the Jacobian matrix of a polynomial map H=(H1,H2,…,Hm)H=(H_{1},H_{2},\ldots,H_{m}):

𝒥​H:=(∂∂x1​H1∂∂x2​H1⋯∂∂xn​H1∂∂x1​H2∂∂x2​H2⋯∂∂xn​H2⋮⋮⋱⋮∂∂x1​Hm∂∂x2​Hm⋯∂∂xn​Hm){\mathcal{J}}H:=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}H_{1}&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}H_{1}&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}H_{1}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}H_{2}&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}H_{2}&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}H_{2}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}H_{m}&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}H_{m}&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}H_{m}\end{array}\right)

Notice that 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H is a row vector if HH is a single polynomial, i.e. m=1m=1.

If we see HH as a column vector, we can evaluate the matrix product 𝒥​H⋅H{\mathcal{J}}H\cdot H, and the characterization of quasi-translations x+Hx+H by Gordan and Nöther comes down to

𝒥​H⋅H=(01,02,…,0n){\mathcal{J}}H\cdot H=(0^{1},0^{2},\ldots,0^{n}) (1.3)

Here, the powers of zero are only taken to indicate the length of the zero vector on the right.

Gordan and Nöther derived the following under the assumption of (1.3). Take a polynomial f∈A⁡[x]f\in A[x] such that 𝒥​f⋅H=0{\mathcal{J}}f\cdot H=0. By the chain rule

𝒥​f​(x+t​H)⋅H\displaystyle{\mathcal{J}}f(x+tH)\cdot H =(𝒥​f)|x=x+t​H⋅(In+t​𝒥​H)⋅H\displaystyle=({\mathcal{J}}f)|_{x=x+tH}\cdot(I_{n}+t{\mathcal{J}}H)\cdot H
=(𝒥​f)|x=x+t​H⋅H=∂∂t​f​(x+t​H)\displaystyle=({\mathcal{J}}f)|_{x=x+tH}\cdot H=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}f(x+tH)

where InI_{n} is the unit matrix of size nn. Here, |x=⋯|_{x=\cdots} means substituting ⋯\cdots for xx. Since 𝒥​f⋅H=0{\mathcal{J}}f\cdot H=0, it follows from the above that

𝒥⁡(f⁡(x+t​H)−f⁡(x))⋅H=∂∂t​f​(x+t​H){\mathcal{J}}\big(f(x+tH)-f(x)\big)\cdot H=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}f(x+tH) (1.4)

Suppose that tt divides the right hand side of (1.4) exactly r<∞r<\infty times. Then tt divides f⁡(x+t​H)−f⁡(x)f(x+tH)-f(x) more than rr times. Hence tt divides the left hand side of (1.4) more than rr times as well, which is a contradiction. So both sides of (1.4) are zero. Since the right hand side of (1.4) is zero and A⊇ℚA\supseteq{\mathbb{Q}}, we get f⁡(x+t​H)=ff(x+tH)=f, and that is what Gordan and Nöther derived from (1.3).

Lemma 1.2.

Assume HH is a polynomial map over AA, such that 𝒥​H⋅H=(01,02,…,0n){\mathcal{J}}H\cdot H=(0^{1},0^{2},\ldots,0^{n}). Then

𝒥​f⋅H=0⟹f⁡(x+t​H)=f⁡(x){\mathcal{J}}f\cdot H=0\Longrightarrow f(x+tH)=f(x) (1.5)

for every f∈A⁡[x]f\in A[x].

With lemmas 1.1 and 1.2, we can prove the following.

Proposition 1.3.

Let AA be a commutative ring with ℚ{\mathbb{Q}} and H:An⇒AnH:A^{n}\Rightarrow A^{n} be a polynomial map. Then the following properties are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation,

  2. (2)

    H⁡(x+t​H)=HH(x+tH)=H, where tt is a new indeterminate,

  3. (3)

    𝒥​H⋅H=(01,02,…,0n){\mathcal{J}}H\cdot H=(0^{1},0^{2},\ldots,0^{n}).

Furthermore,

f⁡(x+H)=f⁡(x)⟺f⁡(x+t​H)=f⁡(x)⟺𝒥​f⋅H=0f(x+H)=f(x)\Longleftrightarrow f(x+tH)=f(x)\Longleftrightarrow{\mathcal{J}}f\cdot H=0 (1.6)

holds for all f∈A⁡[x]f\in A[x], and additionally

(𝒥​H)|x=x−t​𝒥​H=(𝒥​H)+t​(𝒥​H)2+t2​(𝒥​H)3+⋯({\mathcal{J}}H)|_{x=x-t{\mathcal{J}}H}=({\mathcal{J}}H)+t({\mathcal{J}}H)^{2}+t^{2}({\mathcal{J}}H)^{3}+\cdots (1.7)

if any of (1), (2) and (3) is satisfied.

Proof.

The middle hand side of (1.6) gives the left hand side by substituting t=1t=1 and the right hand side by taking the coefficient of t1t^{1}. Hence (1.6) follows from (1) and lemma 1.1 and (3) and lemma 1.2.

By taking the Jacobian of (2), we get (𝒥​H)|x=x+t​H⋅(In+t​𝒥​H)=𝒥​H({\mathcal{J}}H)|_{x=x+tH}\cdot(I_{n}+t{\mathcal{J}}H)={\mathcal{J}}H, which gives (1.7) after substituting t=−tt=-t. Therefore, it remains to show that (1), (2) an (3) are equivalent.

(1) ⇒\Rightarrow (2)

Assume (1). Since x=(x−H)∘(x+H)=x+H−H⁡(x+H)x=(x-H)\circ(x+H)=x+H-H(x+H), we see that H⁡(x+H)=HH(x+H)=H, and (2) follows by taking f=Hif=H_{i} in lemma 1.1.

(2) ⇒\Rightarrow (1)

Assume (2). Then

(x−t​H)∘(x+t​H)\displaystyle(x-tH)\circ(x+tH) =(x+t​H)−t​H​(x+t​H)\displaystyle=(x+tH)-tH(x+tH)
=x+t​H−t​H=x\displaystyle=x+tH-tH=x (1.8)

which gives (1) after substituting t=1t=1.

(2) ⇒\Rightarrow (3)

Assume (2). By taking the coefficient of t1t^{1} of (2), we get (3).

(3) ⇒\Rightarrow (2)

Assume (3). By taking f=Hif=H_{i} in lemma 1.2, we get (2). ∎

Notice that (1.8) tells us that in some sense, x+t​Hx+tH is a quasi-translation as well.

Remark 1.4.

Let DD be the derivation ∑i=1nHi​∂∂xi\sum_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}. Then one can easily verify that

𝒥​f⋅H=0⟺D​f=0{\mathcal{J}}f\cdot H=0\Longleftrightarrow Df=0

and

𝒥​H⋅H=0⟺D2​x1=D2​x2=⋯=D2​xn=0{\mathcal{J}}H\cdot H=0\Longleftrightarrow D^{2}x_{1}=D^{2}x_{2}=\cdots=D^{2}x_{n}=0

Hence quasi-translations correspond to a special kind of locally nilpotent derivations. Furthermore, invariants of the quasi-translation x+Hx+H are just kernel elements of DD.

In addition, we can write exp⁡(D)\exp(D) and exp⁡(t​D)\exp(tD) for the automorphisms corresponding to the maps x+Hx+H and x+t​Hx+tH respectively. But in order to make the article more readable for readers that are not familiar with derivations, we will omit the terminology of derivations further in this article.

2 Singular Hessians and Jacobians

Now that we have had some introduction about quasi-translations, it is time to show how they are connected to singular Hessians. For that purpose, we define the Hessian matrix of a polynomial h∈ℂ⁡[x]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] as follows:

ℋ​h:=(∂∂x1​∂∂x1​h∂∂x2​∂∂x1​h⋯∂∂xn​∂∂x1​h∂∂x1​∂∂x2​h∂∂x2​∂∂x2​h⋯∂∂xn​∂∂x2​h⋮⋮⋱⋮∂∂x1​∂∂xn​h∂∂x2​∂∂xn​h⋯∂∂xn​∂∂xn​h){\mathcal{H}}h:=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}h&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}h&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}h\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}h&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}h&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}h\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}h&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}h&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}h\end{array}\right)

A Hessian is a Jacobian which is symmetric with respect to the main diagonal. Hence each dependence between the columns of a Hessian is also a dependence between the rows of it.

For generality, we consider Jacobians which are not necessary Hessians. Assume G:ℂn→ℂnG:{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}^{n} is a polynomial map and det𝒥​G=0\det{\mathcal{J}}G=0. Let rk⁡M\operatorname{rk}M denote the rank of a matrix MM. It is known that rk⁡𝒥​H=trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H)\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(H), see e.g. Proposition 1.2.9 of either [5] of [1]. Hence there exists a nonzero polynomial R∈ℂ⁡[y]=ℂ⁡[y1,y2,…,yn]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y]={\mathbb{C}}[y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}] such that

R⁡(G1,G2,…,Gn)=0R(G_{1},G_{2},\ldots,G_{n})=0 (2.1)

Here, y1,y2,…,yny_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n} are also variables that correspond to the coordinates of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}. Define

Hi:=(∂R∂yi)|y=GH_{i}:=\Big(\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{i}}\Big)\Big|_{y=G} (2.2)

for all ii. By taking the Jacobian of (2.1), we get

𝒥​0=𝒥⁡(R⁡(G))=(𝒥y​R)|y=G⋅𝒥​G=Ht⋅𝒥​G{\mathcal{J}}0={\mathcal{J}}(R(G))=({\mathcal{J}}_{y}R)|_{y=G}\cdot{\mathcal{J}}G=H^{\rm t}\cdot{\mathcal{J}}G

where Ht=(H1H2⋯Hn)H^{\rm t}=(H_{1}~H_{2}~\cdots~H_{n}) is the transpose of HH. Hence HH is a dependence between the rows of 𝒥​G{\mathcal{J}}G. If 𝒥​G{\mathcal{J}}G is a Hessian, HH is also a dependence between the columns of 𝒥​G{\mathcal{J}}G. Hence it seems a good idea to assume that 𝒥​G⋅H=0{\mathcal{J}}G\cdot H=0. But for the sake of generality, we only assume that 𝒥​G⋅H~=0{\mathcal{J}}G\cdot\tilde{H}=0 for some polynomial vector H~\tilde{H} that does not need to be equal to HH.

If we write ∇yR\nabla_{y}R for the transpose of 𝒥y​R{\mathcal{J}}_{y}R, then H=(∇yR)​(G)H=(\nabla_{y}R)(G), and by the chain rule

𝒥​H⋅H~=𝒥⁡(∇yR)​(G)⋅H~=(𝒥y​∇yR)|y=G⋅𝒥​G⋅H~=0\displaystyle{\mathcal{J}}H\cdot\tilde{H}={\mathcal{J}}(\nabla_{y}R)(G)\cdot\tilde{H}=({\mathcal{J}}_{y}\nabla_{y}R)|_{y=G}\cdot{\mathcal{J}}G\cdot\tilde{H}=0 (2.3)

whence x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation on account of (3) ⇒\Rightarrow (1) of 1.3 if H=H~H=\tilde{H}. Thus we have proved the following.

Proposition 2.1.

Assume HiH_{i} is defined as in (2.2) for each ii, with RR is as in (2.1), where G:ℂn→ℂnG:{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}^{n} is a polynomial map. Then HH is a dependence between the rows of 𝒥​G{\mathcal{J}}G.

If H~\tilde{H} is a dependence between the columns of 𝒥​G{\mathcal{J}}G, then 𝒥​H⋅H~=0{\mathcal{J}}H\cdot\tilde{H}=0. In particular, if HH is a dependence between the columns of 𝒥​G{\mathcal{J}}G, then x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation.

But HH defined as above may be the zero map. This is however not the case if we choose the degree of RR as small as possible, without affecting (2.1), because ∂∂yi​R\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{i}}R is nonzero for some ii and of lower degree than RR itself.

Example 2.2.

Let p=x12​x3+x1​x2​x4+x22​x5p=x_{1}^{2}x_{3}+x_{1}x_{2}x_{4}+x_{2}^{2}x_{5}, h=prh=p^{r} and R=y3​y5−y42R=y_{3}y_{5}-y_{4}^{2}. Then

x+H:=x+(∂R∂y1​(∇h)∂R∂y2​(∇h)∂R∂y3​(∇h)∂R∂y4​(∇h)⋮∂R∂yn−1​(∇h)∂R∂yn​(∇h))=(B⁡(A​x1−B​x2)A⁡(A​x1−B​x2)B⁡(A​x3−B​x4)A⁡(A​x3−B​x4)⋮B⁡(A​xn−1−B​xn)A⁡(A​xn−1−B​xn))x+H:=x+\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{1}}(\nabla h)\\ \frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{2}}(\nabla h)\\ \frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{3}}(\nabla h)\\ \frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{4}}(\nabla h)\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{n-1}}(\nabla h)\\ \frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{n}}(\nabla h)\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}B(Ax_{1}-Bx_{2})\\ A(Ax_{1}-Bx_{2})\\ B(Ax_{3}-Bx_{4})\\ A(Ax_{3}-Bx_{4})\\ \vdots\\ B(Ax_{n-1}-Bx_{n})\\ A(Ax_{n-1}-Bx_{n})\end{array}\right)

is a quasi-translation, and ℋ​h⋅H=(01,02,…,0n){\mathcal{H}}h\cdot H=(0^{1},0^{2},\ldots,0^{n}).

Now let a:=x1​x4−x2​x3a:=x_{1}x_{4}-x_{2}x_{3}, b:=x3​x6−x4​x5b:=x_{3}x_{6}-x_{4}x_{5}, and G:=(∇h)|A=a,B=bG:=(\nabla h)|_{A=a,B=b}. Then R⁡(G)=0R(G)=0 as well. Thus H~:=(∇yR)​(G)=H|A=a,B=b\tilde{H}:=(\nabla_{y}R)(G)=H|_{A=a,B=b} is a dependence between the rows of

3 Hesse’s theorem

A polynomial is homogeneous of degree dd if all its terms have degree dd. A homogeneous polynomial of degree one is called a linear form. We call a quasi-translation x+Hx+H homogeneous if there exists a d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} such that each component HiH_{i} of HH is either zero or homogeneous of degree dd.

When Gordan and Nöther published their article in 1876, it was two years ago that Otto Hesse had died. The role of Hesse is, that the starting point of Gordan and Nöther was a wrong theorem of Hesse, which they proved in dimensions two, three and four, and disproved for all dimensions greater than four.

Hesse’s (invalid) theorem.

Assume n≥2n\geq 2 and hh is a homogeneous polynomial in x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} whose Hessian matrix is singular. Then there is a constant vector c=(c1,c2,…,cn)c=(c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{n}) such that

c1​∂h∂x1+c2​∂h∂x2+⋯+cn​∂h∂xn=0c_{1}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{1}}+c_{2}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{2}}+\cdots+c_{n}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{n}}=0 (3.1)

or equivalently 𝒥​h⋅c=0{\mathcal{J}}h\cdot c=0.

Gordan and Nöther first observe that (3.1) is equivalent to the existence of a linear transformation which makes hh a polynomial in less than nn variables, in other words, the existence of an invertible matrix TT such that

h⁡(T​x)∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn−1]h(Tx)\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-1}]

In order to see that, we first compute the Jacobian matrix of h⁡(T​x)h(Tx) by way of the chain rule, where |x=T​x|_{x=Tx} means substituting the vector T​xTx for xx.

𝒥⁡(h⁡(T​x))=(𝒥​h​(x))|x=T​x⋅T{\mathcal{J}}\big(h(Tx)\big)=\big({\mathcal{J}}h(x)\big)\big|_{x=Tx}\cdot T (3.2)

If the ii-th column of TT is equal to cc, we have

∂∂xi​h​(T​x)=(𝒥​h​(x))|x=T​x⋅c=(∑j=1ncj​∂h∂xj)|x=T​x\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}h(Tx)=\big({\mathcal{J}}h(x)\big)\big|_{x=Tx}\cdot c=\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{j}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{j}}\bigg)\bigg|_{x=Tx}

whence for all c0∈ℂc_{0}\in{\mathbb{C}},

∂∂xi​h​(T​x)=c0⟺∑j=1ncj​∂h∂xj=c0\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}h(Tx)=c_{0}\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{j}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{j}}=c_{0} (3.3)

By taking i=ni=n and c0=0c_{0}=0 in (3.3), we get the above remark of Gordan and Nöther.

We shall prove Hesse’s theorem in dimensions two, three, and four. If we drop the condition that hh is homogeneous, we can prove Hesse’s theorem in dimension two, but only for polynomials hh without linear terms. For polynomials hh with linear terms, we can only get

c1​∂h∂x1+c2​∂h∂x2+⋯+cn​∂h∂xn=c0∈ℂc_{1}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{1}}+c_{2}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{2}}+\cdots+c_{n}\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_{n}}=c_{0}\in{\mathbb{C}}

which holds for homogeneous hh in dimension one as well (h=x1h=x_{1} is homogeneous, but does not satisfy Hesse’s theorem in dimension one). So we will prove the following.

Theorem 3.1.

Hesse’s theorem is true in dimension n≤4n\leq 4, and for non-homogeneous polynomials in dimension n≤2n\leq 2.

Before we prove our affirmative results about Hesse’s theorem, we take a look at the effects of affine transformations of hh and of removing linear terms of hh.

View the vectors x=(x1,x2,…,xn)x=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}), c=(c1,c2,…,cn)c=(c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{n}) and c~=(c~1,c~2,…,c~n)\tilde{c}=(\tilde{c}_{1},\tilde{c}_{2},\ldots,\allowbreak\tilde{c}_{n}) as column matrices of variables and constants respectively. Let TT be an invertible matrix of size nn over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Then

h⁡(T​x+c)h(Tx+c)

is an affine transformation of hh. Write MtM^{\rm t} for the transpose of a matrix MM. Then c~t​x\tilde{c}^{\rm t}x, which is the product of a row matrix and a column matrix, is a matrix with only one entry, and we associate it with the value of its only entry. If we define

h~:=h⁡(T​x+c)−c~t​x\tilde{h}:=h(Tx+c)-\tilde{c}^{\rm t}x

then it appears that detℋ​h~=0\det{\mathcal{H}}\tilde{h}=0, if and only if detℋ​h=0\det{\mathcal{H}}h=0. To see this, notice that on account of (3.2),

𝒥​h~=𝒥⁡(h⁡(T​x+c)−c~t​x)=(𝒥​h)|x=T​x+c⋅T−c~t{\mathcal{J}}\tilde{h}={\mathcal{J}}\big(h(Tx+c)-\tilde{c}^{\rm t}x\big)=({\mathcal{J}}h)|_{x=Tx+c}\cdot T-\tilde{c}^{\rm t}

The transpose of this equals

∇h~=Tt⋅(∇h)|x=T​x+c−c~\nabla\tilde{h}=T^{\rm t}\cdot(\nabla h)|_{x=Tx+c}-\tilde{c}

where ∇f\nabla f stands for the transpose of 𝒥​f{\mathcal{J}}f. Taking the Jacobian of the above, we get

ℋ​h~=ℋ⁡(h⁡(T​x+c)−c~t​x)=𝒥⁡(Tt⋅(∇h)|x=T​x+c−c~)=Tt⋅(ℋ​h)|x=T​x+c⋅T{\mathcal{H}}\tilde{h}={\mathcal{H}}\big(h(Tx+c)-\tilde{c}^{\rm t}x\big)={\mathcal{J}}\big(T^{\rm t}\cdot(\nabla h)|_{x=Tx+c}-\tilde{c}\big)=T^{\rm t}\cdot({\mathcal{H}}h)|_{x=Tx+c}\cdot T

which is a singular matrix, if and only if ℋ​h{\mathcal{H}}h is. If detℋ​h=0\det{\mathcal{H}}h=0, then R⁡(∇h)=0R(\nabla h)=0 for some nonzero R∈ℂ⁡[y]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y] on account of (2.1), and similarly R~​(∇h~)=0\tilde{R}(\nabla\tilde{h})=0.

We shall describe a natural connection between RR and R~\tilde{R}. If R⁡(∇h)=0R(\nabla h)=0 for some R∈ℂ⁡[y]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y], then

R⁡((Tt)−1​((Tt⋅(∇h)|x=T​x+c−c~)+c~))=(R⁡(∇h))|x=T​x+c=0R\Big((T^{\rm t})^{-1}\big((T^{\rm t}\cdot(\nabla h)|_{x=Tx+c}-\tilde{c})+\tilde{c}\big)\Big)=\Big(R(\nabla h)\Big)\Big|_{x=Tx+c}=0

thus R~:=R⁡((Tt)−1​(y−c~))\tilde{R}:=R((T^{\rm t})^{-1}(y-\tilde{c})) satisfies R~​(∇h~)=0\tilde{R}(\nabla\tilde{h})=0.

If we define HiH_{i} as in (2.2) with G=∇hG=\nabla h for each ii, then we get H=(∇yR)​(∇h)H=(\nabla_{y}R)(\nabla h), and x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation on account of corollary 2.1. In a similar manner, x+H~x+\tilde{H} is a quasi-translation if H~=(∇yR~)​(∇h~)\tilde{H}=(\nabla_{y}\tilde{R})(\nabla\tilde{h}), and again we describe a natural connection. By the chain rule,

𝒥y​R~=𝒥y​R​((Tt)−1​(y−c~))=(𝒥y​R)|y=(Tt)−1​(y−c~)⋅(Tt)−1{\mathcal{J}}_{y}\tilde{R}={\mathcal{J}}_{y}R\big((T^{\rm t})^{-1}(y-\tilde{c})\big)=({\mathcal{J}}_{y}R)|_{y=(T^{\rm t})^{-1}(y-\tilde{c})}\cdot(T^{\rm t})^{-1}

whence

∇yR~=T−1​(∇yR)|y=(Tt)−1​(y−c~)\nabla_{y}\tilde{R}=T^{-1}(\nabla_{y}R)|_{y=(T^{\rm t})^{-1}(y-\tilde{c})}

Combining this with ∇h~=Tt⋅(∇h)|x=T​x+c+c~\nabla\tilde{h}=T^{\rm t}\cdot(\nabla h)|_{x=Tx+c}+\tilde{c}, we get that

H~=(∇yR~)​(∇h~)=T−1​H​(T​x+c)\tilde{H}=(\nabla_{y}\tilde{R})(\nabla\tilde{h})=T^{-1}H(Tx+c)

thus H~\tilde{H} is a linear conjugation of HH if c=0c=0. In general,

x+H~=x+T−1​H​(T​x+c)=T−1​((T​x+c+H⁡(T​x+c))−c)x+\tilde{H}=x+T^{-1}H(Tx+c)=T^{-1}\Big(\big(Tx+c+H(Tx+c)\big)-c\Big)

is an affinely linear conjugation of x+Hx+H. In the next section, we shall show that affinely linear conjugations of quasi-translations are again quasi-translations.

We are now ready to prove the following.

Theorem 3.2.

Assume h∈ℂ⁡[x]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] and R≠0R\neq 0 satisfies (2.1) and is of minimum degree. Define H=(∇yR)​(∇h)H=(\nabla_{y}R)(\nabla h).

If hh is homogeneous, then RR and HH are homogeneous as well.

If the dimension of the linear span of the image of HH is at most one, then deg⁡R=1\deg R=1 and x+Hx+H is a regular translation.

Proof.

If hh is homogeneous, then (2.1) is still satisfied if RR is replaced by any homogeneous component of it. Since RR was chosen of minimum degree, we see that RR and hence also HH is homogenous if hh is homogeneous.

Assume that the dimension of the linear span of the image of HH is at most one. Then there are n−1n-1 independent vectors c(i)∈ℂnc^{(i)}\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} such that

(c(1))t​H=(c(2))t​H=⋯=(c(n−1))t​H=0(c^{(1)})^{\rm t}H=(c^{(2)})^{\rm t}H=\cdots=(c^{(n-1)})^{\rm t}H=0

Suppose that deg⁡R≠1\deg R\neq 1. Since (c(i))tH=((c(i))t∇R)(∇h)(c^{(i)})^{\rm t}H=((c^{(i)})^{\rm t}\nabla R)(\nabla h) for each ii and RR is of minimum degree, we have (c(i))t∇R=0(c^{(i)})^{\rm t}\nabla R=0 for each ii. Take an invertible matrix TT over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that the ii-th column of (Tt)−1(T^{\rm t})^{-1} equals c(i)c^{(i)} for each i≤n−1i\leq n-1. Then (𝒥​R)⋅c(i)=0({\mathcal{J}}R)\cdot c^{(i)}=0 for each i≤n−1i\leq n-1. By applying (3.3) with R⁡(y)R(y) instead of h⁡(x)h(x) and c0=0c_{0}=0, we obtain ∂∂yi​R​((Tt)−1​y)=0\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{i}}R\big((T^{\rm t})^{-1}y\big)=0 for all i≤n−1i\leq n-1, so

R~​(y):=R⁡((Tt)−1​y)∈ℂ⁡[yn]\tilde{R}(y):=R\big((T^{\rm t})^{-1}y\big)\in{\mathbb{C}}[y_{n}]

Notice that for h~:=h⁡(T​x)\tilde{h}:=h(Tx), we have R~(∇h~)=R((Tt)−1Tt∇h)|x=T​x=0\tilde{R}(\nabla\tilde{h})=R\big((T^{\rm t})^{-1}T^{\rm t}\nabla h\big)\big|_{x=Tx}=0, whence

∂∂xn​h~\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\tilde{h}

is algebraic over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. This is only possible if this derivative is a constant c0c_{0}, which means that the left hand side of (3.3) holds for i=ni=n. Thus RR can be chosen of degree one, and since that is the minimum possible degree for RR, we have deg⁡R=1\deg R=1 and HH is constant. ∎

Proof of theorem 3.1.

In section 5, we will show that for quasi-translations x+Hx+H in dimension two and for homogeneous quasi-translations x+Hx+H in dimension three, the linear span of the image of HH has dimension at most one. So the case n≤3n\leq 3 of theorem 3.1 follows from theorem 3.2. Additionally, we will show in section 5 that for homogeneous quasi-translations x+Hx+H in dimension n=4n=4, the linear span of the image of HH has dimension at most two. So the case n=4n=4 of theorem 3.1 follows from theorem 3.2 and theorem 3.3 below. ∎

Theorem 3.3.

Assume h∈ℂ⁡[x]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] and R≠0R\neq 0 satisfies (2.1) and is of minimum degree. Define H=(∇yR)​(∇h)H=(\nabla_{y}R)(\nabla h).

If RR is homogeneous, then the dimension of the linear span of the image of HH is not equal to two.

Proof.

Assume that the linear span of the image of HH has dimension two. Then there are n−2n-2 independent vectors c(i)∈ℂnc^{(i)}\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} such that

(c(1))t​H=(c(2))t​H=⋯=(c(n−2))t​H=0(c^{(1)})^{\rm t}H=(c^{(2)})^{\rm t}H=\cdots=(c^{(n-2)})^{\rm t}H=0

Since (c(i))tH=((c(i))t∇R)(∇h)(c^{(i)})^{\rm t}H=((c^{(i)})^{\rm t}\nabla R)(\nabla h) for each ii and RR is of minimum degree, we have (c(i))t∇R=0(c^{(i)})^{\rm t}\nabla R=0 for each ii. Take an invertible matrix TT over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that the ii-th column of (Tt)−1(T^{\rm t})^{-1} equals c(i)c^{(i)} for each i≤n−2i\leq n-2. By applying (3.3) with R⁡(y)R(y) instead of h⁡(x)h(x) and c0=0c_{0}=0, we see that ∂∂yi​R​((Tt)−1​y)=0\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{i}}R\big((T^{\rm t})^{-1}y\big)=0 for all i≤n−2i\leq n-2, so

R~​(y):=R⁡((Tt)−1​y)∈ℂ⁡[yn−1,yn]\tilde{R}(y):=R\big((T^{\rm t})^{-1}y\big)\in{\mathbb{C}}[y_{n-1},y_{n}]

Notice that for h~:=h⁡(T​x)\tilde{h}:=h(Tx), we have R~​(∇h~)=0\tilde{R}(\nabla\tilde{h})=0.

We will show below that Hesse’s theorem holds for h~\tilde{h} and hence also for hh. Consequently, deg⁡R=1\deg R=1 and HH is constant. This contradicts the assumption that the linear span of the image of HH has dimension two.

More precisely, we shall show that there are cn−1,cn∈ℂc_{n-1},c_{n}\in{\mathbb{C}}, not both zero, such that

cn−1​∂∂xn−1​h~+cn​∂∂xn​h~=0c_{n-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n-1}}\tilde{h}+c_{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\tilde{h}=0 (3.4)

The case where ∂∂xn​h~=0\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\tilde{h}=0 is trivial, so assume the opposite. Then

R~​(∂∂xn−1​h~∂∂xn​h~,1)=R~​(∇h~∂∂xn​h~)=R~​(∇h~)(∂∂xn​h~)deg⁡R~=0\tilde{R}\bigg(\frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n-1}}\tilde{h}}{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\tilde{h}},1\bigg)=\tilde{R}\bigg(\frac{\nabla\tilde{h}}{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\tilde{h}}\bigg)=\frac{\tilde{R}(\nabla\tilde{h})}{\big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\tilde{h}\big)^{\deg\tilde{R}}}=0

Thus the quotient of ∂∂xn−1​h~\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n-1}}\tilde{h} and ∂∂xn​h~\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\tilde{h} is algebraic over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, which gives (3.4). ∎

If we take

h=x3​x4andR=y1​y3+y2​y4h=x_{3}x_{4}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad R=y_{1}y_{3}+y_{2}y_{4}

we get H=(x4,x3,0,0)H=(x_{4},x_{3},0,0), and the span of image of HH has dimension two. Thus the condition that RR has minimum degree is necessary in theorem 3.2.

4 Quasi-degrees

Take f∈ℂ⁡[x]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] arbitrary and assume that cc is equal to the ii-th standard basis unit vector. Then

f⁡(x+t​c)|xi=0|t=xi=f⁡(x)f(x+tc)|_{x_{i}=0}\big|_{t=x_{i}}=f(x)

for all ii, whence the degree with respect to xix_{i} of ff is equal to the degree with respect to tt of f⁡(x+t​c)f(x+tc). Based on this property, we define the quasi-degree of a polynomial f∈ℂ⁡[x]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] with respect to a quasi-translation x+Hx+H as the degree with respect to tt of f⁡(x+t​H)f(x+tH):

ν⁡(f):=degt⁡f⁡(x+t​H)\nu(f):=\deg_{t}f(x+tH) (4.1)

A property of ν\nu that follows immediately from the definition is the following.

ν⁡(f​g)=ν⁡(f)+ν⁡(g)\nu(fg)=\nu(f)+\nu(g) (4.2)

The quasi-degree plays an important role in the study of quasi-translations, which the proofs of the following propositions make clear.

Proposition 4.1.

Assume x+g​Hx+gH is a quasi-translation over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, where g∈ℂ⁡[x]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] is nonzero. Then x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} as well, and ν⁡(g)=0\nu(g)=0. Furthermore, the invariants of x+Hx+H are the same as those of x+g​Hx+gH.

Proof.

From (1) ⇒\Rightarrow (2) of proposition 1.3, we deduce that Hi​(x+t​g​H)⋅g⁡(x+t​g​H)=Hi⋅gH_{i}(x+tgH)\cdot g(x+tgH)=H_{i}\cdot g. Substituting t=g−1​tt=g^{-1}t in it and using (4.2) and g≠0g\neq 0, we obtain that

ν⁡(Hi)≤ν⁡(g)+ν⁡(Hi)=ν⁡(g​Hi)≤0\nu(H_{i})\leq\nu(g)+\nu(H_{i})=\nu(gH_{i})\leq 0

for each ii, which is exactly H⁡(x+t​H)=HH(x+tH)=H. Hence x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation on account of (2) ⇒\Rightarrow (1) of proposition 1.3.

Thus it remains to be shown that the invariants of x+Hx+H and x+g​Hx+gH are the same. Assume ff is an invariant of x+Hx+H. Then f⁡(x+t​H)=f⁡(x)f(x+tH)=f(x) on account of (1.6), and by substituting t=gt=g we see that ff is an invariant of x+g​Hx+gH. The converse follows in a similar manner by substituting t=g−1t=g^{-1}. ∎

Notice that proposition 4.1 above gives a tool to obtain quasi-translations x+Hx+H over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} for which gcd⁡{H1,H2,…,Hn}=1\gcd\{H_{1},H_{2},\ldots,H_{n}\}=1 from arbitrary quasi-translations x+Hx+H over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}.

Proposition 4.2.

Assume x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation in dimension nn over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, and FF is an invertible polynomial map in dimension nn over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} with inverse GG. Then

G∘(x+H)∘FG\circ(x+H)\circ F

is a quasi-translation as well, if and only if ν⁡(Gi)≤1\nu(G_{i})\leq 1 for all ii. In particular, if TT is an invertible matrix of size nn over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, we have that

x+T−1​H​(T​x)=T−1​(T​x+H⁡(T​x))=T−1​x∘H∘T​xx+T^{-1}H(Tx)=T^{-1}\big(Tx+H(Tx)\big)=T^{-1}x\circ H\circ Tx

is a quasi-translation as well.

Proof.

Assume first that degt⁡G⁡(x+t​H)≤1\deg_{t}G(x+tH)\leq 1 for all ii. Then we can write

G⁡(x+t​H)=G(0)+t​G(1)G(x+tH)=G^{(0)}+tG^{(1)}

Notice that G(0)=G⁡(x+t​H)|t=0=GG^{(0)}=G(x+tH)|_{t=0}=G. Hence

G∘(x+t​H)∘F=G(0)​(F)+t​G(1)​(F)=G⁡(F)+t​G(1)​(F)=x+t​G(1)​(F)G\circ(x+tH)\circ F=G^{(0)}(F)+tG^{(1)}(F)=G(F)+tG^{(1)}(F)=x+tG^{(1)}(F)

By substituting t=1t=1 on both sides, we obtain that G∘(x+H)∘F=x+G(1)​(F)G\circ(x+H)\circ F=x+G^{(1)}(F) and substituting t=−1t=-1 tells us that its inverse G∘(x−H)∘FG\circ(x-H)\circ F is equal to x−G(1)​(F)x-G^{(1)}(F). Thus G∘(x+H)∘FG\circ(x+H)\circ F is a quasi-translation.

Assume next that G∘(x+H)∘FG\circ(x+H)\circ F is a quasi-translation x+H~x+\tilde{H}. Then

H~=(G∘(x+H)∘F)−x=x−(G∘(x−H)∘F)\tilde{H}=(G\circ(x+H)\circ F)-x=x-(G\circ(x-H)\circ F)

Substituting x=G⁡(x+m​H)x=G(x+mH) in the above gives

5 Quasi-translations with small Jacobian rank

Proposition 5.1 below gives a tool to obtain homogeneous quasi-translations over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} from arbitrary quasi-translations x+Hx+H over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Hence we can obtain results about arbitrary quasi-translations by studying homogeneous ones.

Proposition 5.1.

Assume x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} in dimension nn, and

d≥deg⁡H:=max⁡{deg⁡H1,deg⁡H2,…,deg⁡Hn}d\geq\deg H:=\max\{\deg H_{1},\deg H_{2},\ldots,\deg H_{n}\}

Proof.

Notice that H~\tilde{H} is indeed polynomial and homogeneous of degree dd.

    We show that x~+H~\tilde{x}+\tilde{H} is a quasi-translation in dimension n+1n+1 over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}.     Using 𝒥​H~n+1=0{\mathcal{J}}\tilde{H}_{n+1}=0 and factoring out xn+12​d−1x_{n+1}^{2d-1}, we see that it suffices to show that

    =(𝒥​H⋅xn+1−1⋅xn+1​H)x=xn+1−1​x\displaystyle=({\mathcal{J}}H\cdot x_{n+1}^{-1}\cdot x_{n+1}H)_{x=x_{n+1}^{-1}x}
    =𝒥⁡(H⁡(xn+1−1​x))⋅xn+1​H​(xn+1−1​x)∎\displaystyle={\mathcal{J}}\big(H(x_{n+1}^{-1}x)\big)\cdot x_{n+1}H(x_{n+1}^{-1}x)\qed
  2. (ii)

    We show that rk⁡𝒥​H≤rk⁡𝒥x~​H~≤rk⁡𝒥​H+1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}_{\tilde{x}}\tilde{H}\leq\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H+1. Hence it suffices to show that trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H)≤trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H~)≤trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H)+1\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(H)\leq\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(\tilde{H})\leq\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(H)+1.

    If R⁡(H~)=0R(\tilde{H})=0 for some polynomial R∈ℂ⁡[y]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y], then substituting xn+1=1x_{n+1}=1 gives R⁡(H)=0R(H)=0. Hence trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H)≤trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H~)\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(H)\leq\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(\tilde{H}). If R⁡(H)=0R(H)=0 for some polynomial R∈ℂ⁡[y]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y], say of degree rr, then R~:=yn+1r​R​(yn+1−1​y)\tilde{R}:=y_{n+1}^{r}R(y_{n+1}^{-1}y) satisfies R~​(H~,xn+1d)=0\tilde{R}(\tilde{H},x_{n+1}^{d})=0. Gordan and Nöther used techniques of algebraic geometry to obtain results about homogeneous quasi-translation. They found the following property of homogeneous quasi-translations x+Hx+H:

H⁡(t​H)=0H(tH)=0 (5.1)

This equality can be obtained by looking at the leading coefficient of tt in H⁡(x+t​H)=HH(x+tH)=H, which is (2) of proposition 1.3.

Below we will give algebraic proofs of the results of Gordan and Nöther about homogeneous quasi-translations with Jacobian rank at most 22, especially theorem 5.3 below.

Theorem 5.2.

Assume x+Hx+H is a homogeneous quasi-translation in dimension nn over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Then rk⁡𝒥​H≤1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq 1, if and only if H=g​cH=gc for some g∈ℂ⁡[x]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] and a vector c∈ℂnc\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}. If HH is not of the above form, then 2≤rk⁡𝒥​H≤n−22\leq\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq n-2. In particular, n≥4n\geq 4 in that case.

Proof.

If H=g​cH=gc, then 𝒥​H=c⋅𝒥​g{\mathcal{J}}H=c\cdot{\mathcal{J}}g and therefore rk⁡𝒥​H≤1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq 1. Then there exists a j≤nj\leq n such that g:=Hj≠0g:=H_{j}\neq 0. If for all i≤ni\leq n and for each f∈ℂ⁡[x]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x], ff divides HiH_{i} at least as many times as it divides gg, then H=g​cH=gc for some g∈ℂ⁡[x]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] and a vector c∈ℂnc\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}. So take any i≤ni\leq n and any f∈ℂ⁡[x]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x].

It is known that rk⁡𝒥​H=trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H)\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(H), see e.g. Proposition 1.2.9 of either [5] of [1]. Since trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H)=rk⁡𝒥​H=1\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(H)=\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=1, there exists a nonzero polynomial R∈ℂ⁡[y1,y2]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y_{1},y_{2}] such that R⁡(Hi,Hj)=0R(H_{i},H_{j})=0. Since HH is homogeneous, we can replace RR by one of its homogeneous components, so we may assume that RR is homogeneous. If ff divides HiH_{i} fewer times than it divides g=Hjg=H_{j}, then the number of times that ff divides R⁡(Hi,Hj)R(H_{i},H_{j}) is determined by the nonzero term of lowest degree with respect to y2y_{2} of RR, which leads to a contradiction. So H=g​cH=gc for some g∈ℂ⁡[x]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] and a vector c∈ℂnc\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, if and only if rk⁡𝒥​H≤1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq 1.

Assume next that HH is not of the form g​cgc for any g∈ℂ⁡[x]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] and any vector c∈ℂnc\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}. Let g=gcd⁡{H1,H2,…,Hn}g=\gcd\{H_{1},H_{2},\ldots,H_{n}\} and define H~=g−1​H\tilde{H}=g^{-1}H. On account of proposition 4.1, x+H~x+\tilde{H} is a homogenous quasi-translation as well, and by assumption, there is no c∈ℂnc\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} such that H~=c\tilde{H}=c, i.e. H~\tilde{H} is not constant. From (5.1), we deduce that H~i​(H~)=0\tilde{H}_{i}(\tilde{H})=0 for each ii. Hence also H~i​(H)=0\tilde{H}_{i}(H)=0 for each ii.

Now suppose that rk⁡𝒥​H=n−1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=n-1. Then trdegℂ⁡ℂ⁡(H)=n−1\operatorname{trdeg}_{{\mathbb{C}}}{\mathbb{C}}(H)=n-1 as well, so the prime ideal 𝔭:={R∈ℂ⁡[y]∣R⁡(H)=0}\mathfrak{p}:=\{R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y]\mid R(H)=0\} has height n−(n−1)=1n-(n-1)=1. Since ℂ⁡[y]{\mathbb{C}}[y] is a unique factorization domain, it follows that 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is principal. Theorem 5.3 is somewhat deeper and based on techniques in the paper [8] by Gordan and Nöther, see also [9]. [2, Th. 3.6 (iii)] contains another proof of the assertion that s≥2s\geq 2 in theorem 5.3 below, which is sufficient to obtain theorem 3.1.

So we may assume that H1=H2=⋯=Hs=0H_{1}=H_{2}=\cdots=H_{s}=0 and Hs+1,Hs+2,…,HnH_{s+1},H_{s+2},\ldots,H_{n} are linearly independent over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} for some s≥0s\geq 0. Let θ∈V⁡(ϕ(L′))\theta\in V(\phi^{(L^{\prime})}) and c:=H⁡(θ)c:=H(\theta). If cc is the zero vector, then Hi​(θ)=0H_{i}(\theta)=0. Lemma 5.4.

Let HH be a homogeneous polynomial map of degree dd over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, such that rk⁡𝒥​H=2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=2. Then the image of HH consists of a union of lines through the origin.

Theorem 5.5.

Assume x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that rk⁡𝒥​H=1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=1. Then the linear span of the image of HH has dimension n−1n-1 at most.

Proof.

Just as in the proof of theorem 5.3, we may assume that H1=H2=⋯=Hs=0H_{1}=H_{2}=\cdots=H_{s}=0 and Hs+1,Hs+2,…,HnH_{s+1},H_{s+2},\ldots,H_{n} are linearly independent over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} for some s≥1s\geq 1. If Hn=1H_{n}=1, then define n~=n+1\tilde{n}=n+1 and let H~\tilde{H} be the homogeneization of HH as in proposition 5.1. If Hn=1H_{n}=1, then define n~=n+2\tilde{n}=n+2 and let H~\tilde{H} be the homogeneization of (H,1)(H,1) as in proposition 5.1. Let x~=(x1,x2,…,xn~)\tilde{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{\tilde{n}}). Since (x,xn+1)+(H,1)(x,x_{n+1})+(H,1) is a quasi-translation as well, it follows from proposition 5.1 that x~+H~\tilde{x}+\tilde{H} is also a quasi-translation, and that rk⁡𝒥x~​H~≤rk⁡𝒥​H+1=2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}_{\tilde{x}}\tilde{H}\leq\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H+1=2.

One can easily verify that gcd⁡{H~1,H~2,…,H~n~}=1\gcd\{\tilde{H}_{1},\tilde{H}_{2},\ldots,\tilde{H}_{\tilde{n}}\}=1 and that H~s+1,H~s+2,…,H~n~−1\tilde{H}_{s+1},\tilde{H}_{s+2},\allowbreak\ldots,\tilde{H}_{\tilde{n}-1} are linearly independent over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Hence rk⁡𝒥​H~=2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}\tilde{H}=2 on account of theorem 5.2. By interchanging coordinates s+1s+1 and n~\tilde{n}, we can deduce from theorem 5.3 that s≥1s\geq 1 and that H~i∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xs,xn~]\tilde{H}_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,\allowbreak x_{s},x_{\tilde{n}}]. Hence Hi∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xs]H_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{s}] for each ii. ∎

Corollary 5.6.

Assume x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation in dimension nn.

  1. (i)

    If n≤3n\leq 3, then the linear span of the image of HH has dimension at most max⁡{n−1,1}\max\{n-1,1\}.

  2. (ii)

    If HH is homogeneous and n≤4n\leq 4, then the linear span of the image of HH has dimension at most max⁡{n−2,1}\max\{n-2,1\}.

In particular, the dimension of the linear span of the image of HH is at most 22 if either (i) or (ii) is satisfied.

Proof.

Notice that (i) follows from (ii) by applying (ii) on the homogeneization of HH as in proposition 5.1. So assume that HH is homogeneous and n≤4n\leq 4. Then it follows from theorem 5.2 that either rk⁡𝒥​H≤1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq 1 or 2≤rk⁡𝒥​H≤n−2≤22\leq\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq n-2\leq 2. So rk⁡𝒥​H≤2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq 2.

Suppose first that rk⁡𝒥​H≤1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq 1. Then we can deduce from theorem 5.2 that the linear span of the image of HH is generated by a vector cc, so that it has dimension at most 11. Suppose next that rk⁡𝒥​H=2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=2. Then we can deduce from theorem 5.3 that the linear span of the image of HH has dimension at most n−2n-2. ∎

Notice that example 4.3 (in dimension 4) and its homogeneization (in dimension 5) show that the bounds on nn in (i) and (ii) of the above corollary are sharp. Example 2.3 shows that for homogeneous quasi-translations, the linear span of the image of HH may have dimension nn.

Corollary 5.6 tells what the dimension of the linear span of HH is, but not how HH looks. Since the dimension of the linear span of HH is at most 22, we may assume that H1=H2=⋯=Hn−2=0H_{1}=H_{2}=\cdots=H_{n-2}=0 on account of proposition 4.2, so that we can apply the following theorem.

Theorem 5.7.

Assume x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation, such that H1=H2=⋯=Hn−2=0H_{1}=H_{2}=\cdots=H_{n-2}=0. Then HH is of the form

H=(01,02,…,0n−2,b​g,a​g)H=\big(0^{1},0^{2},\ldots,0^{n-2},b\,g,a\,g\big)

where g∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn−2,a​xn−1−b​xn]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2},a\,x_{n-1}-b\,x_{n}] and a,b∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn−2]a,b\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2}].

Proof.

Let g=gcd⁡{Hn−1,Hn}g=\gcd\{H_{n-1},H_{n}\} and take b=g−1​Hn−1b=g^{-1}H_{n-1} and a=g−1​Hn−1a=g^{-1}H_{n-1}. We first show that a,b∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn−2]a,b\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2}]. We distinguish two cases.

  • •

    rk⁡𝒥​H≤1\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq 1.
    If Hn−1H_{n-1} and HnH_{n} are linearly independent over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, then we can deduce from theorem 5.5 that Hn−1,Hn∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn−2]H_{n-1},H_{n}\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2}], so that a,b∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn−2]a,b\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\allowbreak\ldots,\allowbreak x_{n-2}] as well. If Hn−1H_{n-1} and HnH_{n} are linearly dependent over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, but not both equal to zero, then a,b∈ℂa,b\in{\mathbb{C}} because gcd⁡{a,b}=1\gcd\{a,b\}=1 and a​Hn−1−b​Hn=0aH_{n-1}-bH_{n}=0 is a linear dependence of Hn−1H_{n-1} and HnH_{n} over ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn−2]{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2}].

  • •

    rk⁡𝒥​H=2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=2.
    Let g=gcd⁡{Hn−1,Hn}g=\gcd\{H_{n-1},H_{n}\}. From proposition 4.1, it follows that x+g−1​Hx+g^{-1}H is a quasi-translation as well. Furthermore, gg is an invariant of x+g−1​Hx+g^{-1}H. Let H~\tilde{H} be the homogeneization of g−1​Hg^{-1}H. Just like in the last paragraph of the proof of theorem 5.5, we can deduce that b=g−1​Hn−1b=g^{-1}H_{n-1} and a=g−1​Hn−1a=g^{-1}H_{n-1} are contained in ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn−2]{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2}].

Since gg is an invariant of x+g−1​Hx+g^{-1}H, it follows from (1.6) in proposition 1.3 that

b​∂∂xn−1​g+a​∂∂xn​g=0b\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n-1}}g+a\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}g=0 (5.4)

If we express gg as a polynomial in ℂ⁡(x1,x2,…,xn−2)​[a​xn−1−b​xn,xi]{\mathbb{C}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n-2})[a\,x_{n-1}-b\,x_{n},x_{i}] for some i∈{n−1,n}i\in\{n-1,n\}, then we can deduce from equation (5.4) that g∈ℂ⁡(x1,x2,…,xn−2)​[a​xn−1−b​xn]g\in{\mathbb{C}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,\allowbreak x_{n-2})[a\,x_{n-1}-b\,x_{n}].

The following results follow immediately from corollary 5.6 and theorems 5.5 and 5.7.

Corollary 5.8 (Z. Wang).

Assume x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation in dimension n≤3n\leq 3 over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Then there exists an invertible matrix TT over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that T−1​H​(T​x)T^{-1}H(Tx) is of the form

  1. (1)

    (0,g)(0,g), where g∈ℂ⁡[x1]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1}], if n=2n=2,

  2. (2)

    (0,b​g,a​g)(0,b\,g,a\,g), where g∈ℂ⁡[x1,a​x2−b​x3]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},a\,x_{2}-b\,x_{3}] and a,b∈ℂ⁡[x1]a,b\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1}], if n=3n=3.

Corollary 5.9.

Assume x+Hx+H is a homogeneous quasi-translation in dimension n≤4n\leq 4 over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Then there exists an invertible matrix TT over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that T−1​H​(T​x)T^{-1}H(Tx) is of the form

  1. (1)

    (0,0,g)(0,0,g), where g∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2}], if n=3n=3,

  2. (2)

    (0,0,b​g,a​g)(0,0,b\,g,a\,g), where g∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,a​x3−b​x4]g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},a\,x_{3}-b\,x_{4}] and a,b∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2]a,b\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2}], if n=4n=4.

Theorem 5.3 was proved first by Gordan and Nöther in [8]. Corollary 5.8 was proved first by Wang in [11].

Remark 5.10.

If x+Hx+H is a homogeneous quasi-translation such that rk⁡𝒥​H=2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=2, then x+g​Hx+gH does not need to be a quasi-translation. For homogeneous maps HH with rk⁡𝒥​H=2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=2, x+g−1​Hx+g^{-1}H is a quasi-translation for some polynomial gg, if and only if 𝒥​H⋅H=tr⁡𝒥​H⋅H{\mathcal{J}}H\cdot H=\operatorname{tr}{\mathcal{J}}H\cdot H, i.e. at most one of the eigenvalues of 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H is nonzero, see [1, Th. 4.5.2]. If 𝒥​H⋅H=0{\mathcal{J}}H\cdot H=0, then it follows from (1.7) in proposition 1.3 that 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H is nilpotent, i.e. all eigenvalues of 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H are zero.

6 Results and questions

Gordan and Nöther classified all homogeneous polynomials with singular Hessians in dimension five as follows.

Theorem 6.1 (Gordan and Nöther).

Assume h∈ℂ⁡[x]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] is a homogeneous polynomial in dimension n=5n=5. If detℋ​h=0\det{\mathcal{H}}h=0 and hh does not satisfy Hesse’s theorem, then there exists an invertible matrix TT over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that h⁡(T​x)h(Tx) is of the form

h⁡(T​x)=f⁡(x1,x2,a1​x3+a2​x4+a3​x5)h(Tx)=f\big(x_{1},x_{2},a_{1}x_{3}+a_{2}x_{4}+a_{3}x_{5}\big)

where f∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}] and a1,a2,a3∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2]a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2}].

This result can also be found in [6], [7, §4], and as [2, Th. 4.1]. Theorem 6.1 has a non-homogeneous variant, namely [3, Th. 3.3], which is as follows.

Theorem 6.2.

Assume h∈ℂ⁡[x]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] is a polynomial in dimension n=3n=3. If detℋ​h=0\det{\mathcal{H}}h=0 and hh does not satisfy Hesse’s theorem, then there exists an invertible matrix TT over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that h⁡(T​x)h(Tx) is of the form

h⁡(T​x)=a1+a2​x2+a3​x3h(Tx)=a_{1}+a_{2}x_{2}+a_{3}x_{3}

where a1,a2,a3∈ℂ⁡[x1]a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1}].

The results of theorems 3.1 and 6.2 for polynomials in nn variables with singular Hessians can be generalized to polynomials with Hessian rank n−1n-1, as has been done in Theorems 5.3.5 and 5.3.10 in [1]. But the results of theorem 3.1 and [3, Th. 3.5] admit a similar genralization. Furthermore, one may replace ℂ{\mathbb{C}} by any field of characteristic zero in all of the above. These results will appear in a future paper by the author.

In dimension four, only those hh for which there exists a nonzero R∈ℂ⁡[y1,y2,y3,y4]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y_{1},y_{2},\allowbreak y_{3},y_{4}] with R⁡(∇h)=0R(\nabla h)=0, such that

c1​∂R∂y1+c2​∂R∂y2+c3​∂R∂y3+c4​∂R∂y4=0c_{1}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{1}}+c_{2}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{2}}+c_{3}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{3}}+c_{4}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{4}}=0

for some nonzero c∈ℂ4c\in{\mathbb{C}}^{4}, are known. See [1, Th. 5.3.3] or [3, Th. 3.5]. This leads to the following question.

Problem 1.

Assume h∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}] such that detℋ​h=0\det{\mathcal{H}}h=0. Does there exist a nonzero R∈ℂ⁡[y1,y2,y3,y4]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{4}] such that R⁡(∇h)=0R(\nabla h)=0 and

c1​∂R∂y1+c2​∂R∂y2+c3​∂R∂y3+c4​∂R∂y4=0c_{1}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{1}}+c_{2}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{2}}+c_{3}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{3}}+c_{4}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{4}}=0

for some c∈ℂ4c\in{\mathbb{C}}^{4}?

The one who first solves this problem receives a bottle of Joustra Beerenburg (Frisian spirit). Problem 2 below generalizes problem 1. Indeed, suppose that ff is a counterexample to problem 1. Then it is known that the RR in problem 1 cannot be homogeneous, which is in fact the equivalent of problem 2 in dimension four instead of five. From that, one can deduce that f+x5f+x_{5} is a counterexample to problem 2.

Problem 2.

Assume h∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4,x5]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},x_{5}] such that R⁡(∇h)=0R(\nabla h)=0 for some nonzero homogeneous R∈ℂ⁡[y1,y2,y3,y4,y5]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{4},y_{5}]. Is

c1​∂R∂y1+c2​∂R∂y2+c3​∂R∂y3+c4​∂R∂y4+c5​∂R∂y5=0c_{1}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{1}}+c_{2}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{2}}+c_{3}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{3}}+c_{4}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{4}}+c_{5}\frac{\partial R}{\partial y_{5}}=0

for some c∈ℂ5c\in{\mathbb{C}}^{5}?

Quasi-translations in dimension four and homogeneous quasi-translations in dimension five are not classified. For quasi-translations x+Hx+H in dimension five, one can show that rk⁡𝒥​H≤2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H\leq 2 if HH is constructed as H=(∇R)​(∇h)H=(\nabla R)(\nabla h) for a homogeneous h∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,x3,x4,x5]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},x_{5}] and any R∈ℂ⁡[y1,y2,y3,y4,y5]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{4},y_{5}] such that R⁡(∇h)=0R(\nabla h)=0. This is what Gordan and Nöther actually did to get theorem 6.1, see also the proof of [2, Th. 4.1].

The quasi-translation x+H~x+\tilde{H} in example 4.3 has the property that the linear span of the image of H~\tilde{H} has dimension nn. Hence one can ask the following.

Problem 1.

Assume x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation in dimension n=4n=4 such that H=(∇R)​(∇h)H=(\nabla R)(\nabla h) for some h∈ℂ⁡[x]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] and an R∈ℂ⁡[y]R\in{\mathbb{C}}[y] satisfying R⁡(∇h)=0R(\nabla h)=0. Is the dimension of the linear span of the image of HH less than n=4n=4?

If you think that you have seen problem 1 before, you are quite right. Both problems 1 are equivalent.

The quasi-translation of example 4.3 in dimension n=4n=4 is not homogeneous, but the quasi-translation of example 2.3 in dimension n=6n=6 is indeed homogeneous, and the linear span of the image of HH has dimension nn as well. Since the linear span of the image of HH has dimension less than nn if n≤3n\leq 3 and dimension less than n−1n-1 if HH is homogeneous and 3≤n≤43\leq n\leq 4, we have the following question.

Problem 3.

Assume x+Hx+H is a homogeneous quasi-translation in dimension n=5n=5. Is the dimension of the linear span of the image of HH less than 55?

Also for this problem, the one who first solves it receives a bottle of Joustra Beerenburg (Frisian spirit).

For a counterexample to problem 3, we would have rk⁡𝒥​H=3\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=3. Gordan and Nöther divide the homogeneous quasi-translations x+Hx+H in dimension five with rk⁡𝒥​H=3\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{J}}H=3 in two groups, which they indicate as ‘Fall a)’ and ‘Fall b)’. They prove that for all ‘Fall a)’ quasi-translations x+Hx+H, the linear span of the image of HH is indeed less than five. The homogeneization of example 4.3 appears to be a ‘Fall b)’ quasi-translation. See [2], in particular section 5 of it, for more information about ‘Fall b)’ quasi-translations x+Hx+H and problem 3.

As observed earlier, 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H is nilpotent if x+Hx+H is a quasi-translation, because of (1.7) in proposition 1.3. Taking about nilpotent matrices, one can wonder how polynomials hh with a nilpotent Hessian look if the dimension or the Jacobian rank is small.

Theorem 6.3.

Assume h∈ℂ⁡[x]h\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] is not necessarily homogeneous, such that ℋ​h{\mathcal{H}}h is nilpotent. Then Hesse’s theorem holds in the following cases.

  1. (i)

    rk⁡ℋ​h≤2\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{H}}h\leq 2 or n≤4n\leq 4,

  2. (ii)

    hh is homogeneous and n=5n=5 (in addition to rk⁡ℋ​h≤3\operatorname{rk}{\mathcal{H}}h\leq 3, in particular n≤4n\leq 4, for which detℋ​h=0\det{\mathcal{H}}h=0 is sufficient).

but there is a counterexample in dimension 66 and a homogeneous counterexample in dimension 1010.

Proof.

(i) and (ii) follow from [1, Th. 5.7.1]. See the beginning of [1, §5.7] for how the counterexamples can be obtained. ∎
